summary: Psalm 113 opens by calling Yahweh’s servants to praise his name now, forever, and across the whole course of the day. It then sets Yahweh’s height above nations and heavens beside his attention to earth. The final movement praises him as the one who raises the poor and needy and gives the barren woman a joyful home.
whyItMatters: This psalm belongs in Book V, where praise becomes an increasingly central response. It gives a compact picture of praise rooted both in God’s exalted rule and in his care for lowly people.

context.author: No individual author is named in the chapter; Psalms as a book is an anthology with many writers and collections.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later received by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalter contains poems from different periods and was formed as a later anthology; one date for Psalm 113 is not established by the chapter.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, a section marked by thanksgiving, Hallel, pilgrimage songs, Torah meditation, and widening praise.
context.literaryForm: Short Hebrew praise poem, using repeated summons, parallel lines, rhetorical question, and vivid reversals.

outline.heading: Call to Praise
outline.note: The psalm summons Yahweh’s servants to praise Yahweh’s name across time and from sunrise to sunset.

outline.heading: The High God Who Looks Down
outline.note: Yahweh is described as above all nations and heavens, yet as one who stoops to see heaven and earth.

outline.heading: The Lowly Lifted
outline.note: The poor and needy are raised from dust and ash heap to sit with princes.

outline.heading: The Barren Woman Settled
outline.note: The psalm ends with a barren woman made joyful in her home, then returns to praise.

keyVerses.text: From the rising of the sun to its going down, Yahweh’s name is to be praised.
keyVerses.why: This line expands the call to praise across the whole visible day, giving the psalm a broad horizon.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh is high above all nations, his glory above the heavens.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the psalm’s claim that Yahweh’s greatness is not limited by any nation or by the heavens.

keyVerses.text: who stoops down to see in heaven and on the earth?
keyVerses.why: The verse connects divine height with divine attention; the God seated high is not distant from what is low.

keyVerses.text: He raises up the poor out of the dust, and lifts up the needy from the ash heap,
keyVerses.why: This begins the psalm’s concrete picture of reversal for people in weakness or disgrace.

questions.question: Who is being told to praise in this psalm?
questions.answer: Verse 1 directly addresses “you servants of Yahweh.” The psalm does not define the group further, but within Psalms such language naturally fits worshipers who belong to Yahweh and are summoned to speak praise.

questions.question: What does “Praise Yah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Praise Yah” is both the opening and closing phrase of the psalm. The Hebrew expression hallelu-yah means “praise Yah,” a plural command using a shortened form of the divine name. Here it frames the whole poem as a call to praise rather than as private reflection only.

questions.question: Why does the psalm keep saying Yahweh’s name?
questions.answer: The chapter praises “Yahweh’s name” in verses 1, 2, and 3. In the poem, the name represents Yahweh as the one to be blessed and praised; the psalm does not separate praise of the name from praise of Yahweh himself.

questions.question: Does “from the rising of the sun to its going down” mean every place or every time of day?
questions.answer: The phrase can be heard spatially, from east to west, and temporally, from morning to evening. The verse itself stresses the breadth of praise without spelling out one exclusive meaning. Readers differ on which emphasis is primary, but both fit the line’s expansive force.

questions.question: How can Yahweh be high above the heavens and still stoop down to see?
questions.answer: Verses 4-6 hold those ideas together. Yahweh is described as exalted above nations and heavens, yet also as one who “stoops down to see” heaven and earth. The point is not that distance prevents care, but that the highly exalted God attends to what is below.

questions.question: What is the force of the question, “Who is like Yahweh, our God?”
questions.answer: The question in verse 5 expects the answer that no one is like Yahweh. It introduces the contrast between his seat “on high” and his stooping attention in verse 6. The psalm uses the question to move from praise of God’s greatness to praise of his care.

questions.question: What do dust and ash heap suggest?
questions.answer: Verse 7 places the poor and needy in images of lowliness: dust and an ash heap. The psalm does not give a biography of a particular person; it uses concrete pictures of humiliation or destitution to describe the kind of reversal Yahweh brings.

questions.question: Does the psalm say every poor person becomes a prince?
questions.answer: The psalm says Yahweh “raises up the poor” and “lifts up the needy,” setting such a person “with princes.” It is a praise poem using reversal language, not a case record that explains when or how every instance happens. Readers should let the image show Yahweh’s care for the lowly without turning it into a simple formula.

questions.question: How should readers hear the line about the barren woman?
questions.answer: Verse 9 presents the barren woman settled in her home as “a joyful mother of children.” In the world of the psalm, childlessness is pictured as grief reversed into joy, but the verse does not explain every experience of infertility or make a rule about all families. It is one final example of Yahweh’s care for someone in a vulnerable or sorrowful place.

glossary.def: A shortened form of the divine name used in the command “Praise Yah” at the beginning and end of the psalm.
The people addressed in verse 1, called to praise Yahweh’s name.
The beginning point in verse 3’s image of praise stretching from sunrise to sunset.
The low place from which Yahweh lifts the needy in verse 7.
The woman in verse 9 whose sorrow is pictured as being changed into joy in her home.
